articles.excerpt: Introduction & Quick Summary Symptom. With Cache Components enabled, next build stops on a route that worked in development: Error: Route "/products/[id]": Next.js encountered uncached or runtime data…
articles.body: Introduction & Quick Summary Symptom. With Cache Components enabled, next build stops on a route that worked in development: Error: Route "/products/[id]": Next.js encountered uncached or runtime data during prerendering. `fetch(...)`, `cookies()`, `headers()`, `params`, `searchParams`, or `connection()` accessed outside of `<Suspense>` prevents the route from being prerendered. Ways to fix this: - [stream] Provide a placeholder with `<Suspense fallback={...}>` around the data access - [cache] For uncached data (`fetch`, database calls): cache the access with `"use cache"` - [block] Set `export const instant = false` to allow a blocking route Cause. cacheComponents: true changes what a build means.

articles.title: Running ARM64 Android games on Apple Silicon without instruction translation
articles.excerpt: Apple Silicon and phone chips share the same instruction set, ARM64. That means a Mac can boot an ARM64 Android system under hardware virtualization and run game code as is, with no x86-to-ARM transla…
articles.body: Apple Silicon and phone chips share the same instruction set, ARM64. That means a Mac can boot an ARM64 Android system under hardware virtualization and run game code as is, with no x86-to-ARM translation layer in between. APK PlayStudio is an Android game emulator built on that idea, coming soon to the Mac App Store. Here is how the stack fits together and what turned out to be hard. The basic stack CPU : QEMU's virt machine with -accel hvf (Hypervisor.framework). One process per emulator, controlled by the Swift app over QMP; frames come back through IOSurface shared memory with zero copies. Touch : QEMU's virtio-multitouch device, driven directly over QMP input-send-event .

articles.title: first-name keeps the hyphen in the draft
articles.excerpt: A key named first-name looks fine in JSON. The drafts do not treat it the same way. On the JSON converter, Laravel quotes it and stays valid. TypeScript and the PHP DTO keep the hyphen in the identifi…
articles.body: A key named first-name looks fine in JSON. The drafts do not treat it the same way. On the JSON converter , Laravel quotes it and stays valid. TypeScript and the PHP DTO keep the hyphen in the identifier. Conversion runs in the browser. Nothing is uploaded. The sample { "first-name" : "Ada" , "role" : "engineer" } Laravel prints valid array syntax: 'first-name' => 'Ada' . TypeScript emits first-name: string; . The PHP DTO emits public string $first-name; and the constructor uses the same name. The class stays DataTransferObject . That is a draft, not production code. Rename the field before you ship if the hyphen is not legal in your language. Keep this separate from other mistakes A trailing comma such as {"a":1,} clears every format. That is a parse error, not a hyphen problem.

articles.title: Trading Strategy Backtest Results: How to Read Them
articles.excerpt: Trading strategy backtest results show how a set of rules would have traded on past prices. They do not show how the same rules will trade next month. A good backtest is a starting point for testing,…
articles.body: Trading strategy backtest results show how a set of rules would have traded on past prices. They do not show how the same rules will trade next month. A good backtest is a starting point for testing, not proof that a bot works. What Backtest Results Really Show A backtest replays your entry and exit rules over historical candles and records the trades. It answers one narrow question: did these rules, on this data, with these assumptions, produce these trades? Every part of that matters. Change the data period, the fees or the rules, and the result can change completely. Backtests are useful because they are cheap and fast. They become misleading when people read them as a forecast.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 19, 2005: Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft makes 1st-ever liftoff from surface of an asteroid
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Hayabusa was supposed to return asteroid samples to Earth. Asteroids are space rocks that were formed during the early solar system. We study asteroids to learn more about the solar system's history. Hayabusa (pronounced HI-uh-BOOS-uh) made two touchdowns on asteroid Itokawa (EE -toh-KA-wah). Each time, the spacecraft went into safe mode. Controllers weren't sure if Hayabusa gathered any material. But they sent the spacecraft back to Earth anyway. Hayabusa's sample return capsule returned to Earth in June 2010 . Scientists found dust of Itokawa inside the capsule, proving that it did indeed capture samples of Itokawa.

articles.excerpt: Japan's space agency has decided to switch destinations and objectives for the final act of its Hayabusa2 asteroid mission, due to problems with the spacecraft's ion thrusters.
articles.body: Japan's space agency has decided to switch destinations and objectives for the final act of its Hayabusa2 mission, due to the spacecraft suffering trouble with its ion thrusters. The veteran Hayabusa2 spacecraft launched back in 2014 to collect material from the asteroid Ryugu . Since delivering the samples to Earth in December 2020 via a reentry capsule, the main spacecraft has been conducting an extended mission of exploration and in July made a super-close flyby of the two-headed asteroid Torifune. But Hayabusa2's continued adventures are now set for a premature end.

articles.title: China rolls out rocket for launch of 1st international astronaut to Tiangong space station (video)
articles.excerpt: China has rolled to the launch pad the rocket and spacecraft for its Shenzhou-24 mission, which will fly the first international astronaut to the nation's Tiangong space station.
articles.body: China's space station is set to receive its first foreign astronaut. A Long March 2F rocket, topped with the Shenzhou-24 crew spacecraft, was rolled out to the pad at Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China, on Tuesday (Nov. 17), with launch expected in the next week. The 191-foot-tall (58 meters) rocket was transferred 0.93 miles (1.5 kilometers) from a vertical integration building to the pad over the course of around two hours, starting around 4 a.m. EST (0900 GMT, or 5 p.m. Beijing Time), according to China Central Television (CCTV). China rolls out the Long March 2F rocket for its Shenzhou-24 astronaut mission on Nov. 17, 2026.
